title: The influence of microstructure on the stress corrosion resistance of SS 304L
abstract: Abstract This study investigated how 304L stainless steel, which is utilized in demanding conditions, is affected by its microstructure in terms of its resistance to stress corrosion cracking (SCC). Through carefully regulated mechanical and thermal processing, researchers created samples with a range of microstructures, which they then characterized using XRD, EBSD, and SEM. Under tensile stress, SCC tests were carried out in an acidic chloride solution in accordance with ASTM G30 recommendations. The findings showed that a fine-grained microstructure limited intergranular corrosion and provided better SCC resistance because of a more uniform chromium distribution. On the other hand, by encouraging localized corrosion and fracture formation, coarser grains and chromium carbides at grain boundaries increased the susceptibility to SCC.
journal: Journal of Materials Science: Materials in Engineering

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: A significant class of engineering materials, stainless steels have found extensive application in a wide range of settings and industries because of their exceptional resistance to oxidation and corrosion. They usually have more than 12% chromium, which gives them corrosion resistance by forming a stubborn, naturally regenerating coating of chromium oxide on their surface. Depending on the application, additional alloying elements including nickel, manganese, and molybdenum are frequently added for various objectives. Additionally, a trace quantity of carbon is present, either as an impurity or as a purposeful addition (Weld and Metall.,  20 ). family of steels known as austenitic stainless steels has a nominal nickel content of 9% and a chromium content of 19%. The most typical microstructural phase in these steels at room temperature is austenite, as the name suggests. The chemical composition can be changed by adding molybdenum to improve resistance to localized corrosion, decreasing the amount of carbon, or adding titanium, niobium, or tantalum to stop chromium carbide from forming (Wanga et al.,  38 ). For use in a variety of industrial sectors, including the dairy, chemical, petrochemical, and biomedical industries as well as steam power generation, austenitic stainless steels are highly sought-after due to their remarkable corrosion resistance, mild ductility, high strength, and reasonable weldability (Karcı et al.,  15 ). One of the various austenitic stainless steel grades in the 300 series, AISI 304L, is used extensively in industries because to its remarkable resistance to corrosion and low-temperature toughness. The estimated yearly usage of austenitic stainless steels 304 and 304L is above 20,000 tons (Smith  33 ).

Austenitic stainless steels (ASSs) have been refined grain-wise thus far using methods like recrystallization (Cao et al.,  7 ), severe plastic deformation (Köhnen et al.,  19 ), and reversion of strain-induced martensite (Lodhi et al.,  22 ). The last method relies on the austenite phase's metastability against strain-induced martensitic transformation during deformation and the martensite's subsequent reversion to ultrafine-grained (UFG) austenite during high-temperature annealing (Yang et al.,  39 ). The stability of the austenite phase is essential for grain refining, where a virtually complete martensitic microstructure is required prior to reverse annealing. Additionally, the transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect, which results in greater ductility during deformation, depends on the stability of the austenite phase (Lodhi et al.,  22 ). The durability of the austenite phase against the martensitic transformation during deformation varies between AISI 304L and 316L stainless steels because of their varied chemical compositions (Miller et al.,  26 ). Herrera et al. looked at the formation of martensite, reversion, and recrystallization in AISI 304L and 316L alloys (Guo et al.,  14 ).

The major failure associated with corrosion under control (CSC) of inoxydable austénitic acids in chlorided environments is still relevant, but recent studies have clarified the mechanisms at work and enhanced surveillance methods, such as using acoustic emission to quickly detect damages (Nuthalapati et al.,  28 ; Taghi Vakili et al.,  35 ). Today's suggested mitigation strategies include judicious selection of the subtlety and state of metallurgy, environmental control (pH, inhibitors, salins/halogénures deposits), and a reduction in contraindications, all supported by more thorough surveillance (Taghi Vakili et al.,  35 ). Regarding AISI 304L, a number of studies demonstrate that the onset of CSC may occur at 45 °C under very low chloride deposits (~ 0,1-1 g-m 3), particularly when hygroscopically based concentration mechanisms are in place (Chun-Ping et al.,  9 ). On the other hand, AISI 316L, which is Mo-enriched, generally exhibits better resistance to piquation and, consequently, a lower risk of CSC caused by the chlorures themselves. However, this benefit is dependent on the microstructure and test conditions and may be confirmed by recent experimental observations (Federal  11 ).

The chemical processing and refinery industries frequently use austenitic stainless steel because of its superior mechanical qualities, heat resistance, weldability, and resistance to corrosion at a variety of elevated temperatures (Proˇsek et al.  30 ). Chloride-induced stress corrosion cracking (CI-SCC) is a cracking process that occurs when a metal is simultaneously exposed to tensile stress and chlorides. It requires a susceptible alloy, a corrosive chloride environment, and tensile stress acting together (Andresen  1 ). Austenitic stainless steels of the 300 series are particularly vulnerable to CI-SCC when they are under tensile stress whether applied or residual. The risk increases in corrosive environments generated by the hydrolysis of calcium, magnesium, and chloride salts (Ford and Andresen  13 ). Boiling a concentrated 44 weight percent MgCl2 solution has been shown to create CI-SCC in stainless steel of the 304L type (Andresen  2 ).

However, the test solution may not reflect real service, where evaporation is limited and chloride levels are only low to moderate. Singh (2004) reported that most SCC failures in gas plants involved 304, 304L, and 316L stainless steels. These failures were driven by chlorides present in moist sour gas (Andresen  3 ), which increased corrosion attacks in environments with 40% relative humidity and 76% relative humidity. The enhanced attack caused slip band attack (Montoya et al.,  27 ) in brines with high magnesium content, resulting in pit-related environmental-assisted microcracking and a change in the cathodic reduction process (Katona et al.,  17 ). These features may indicate hydrogen environment-assisted cracking (HEAC). A plausible contributor is strain-induced martensite formed during rough grinding of the specimen, which can facilitate hydrogen uptake and cracking (Srinivasan et al.,  34 ). With a rough-ground surface, 40% RH ASW exhibited slip-band attack, whereas 76% RH ASW did not. Overall, the type and severity of corrosion damage depend on the brine composition associated with each relative humidity level. (Katona et al.,  18 ).

This work's primary goal is to investigate the tensile test following immersion in seawater and its impact on the microstructure of the steel under mechanical stress to identify the specific degradation processes that may compromise the durability of 304 L stainless steel under these conditions.

sections.heading: Diffractogram of the reference material
paragraphs: The EDS spectrum study in the Fig.  3 , which shows strong peaks for F e  (~ 6.4 keV and ~ 7.1 keV), C r  (~ 5.4 keV and ~ 5.9 keV), and N i  (~ 7.5 keV and ~ 8.3 keV), validates the chemical makeup of 304L stainless steel. These findings are consistent with the alloy's usual composition, in which N i  (8–12%) stabilizes the austenitic phase at ambient temperature and C r  (18–20%) resists corrosion by forming a passive oxide layer (Davis  10 ). Carbon, which is essential for mechanical strength but needs to be carefully controlled to avoid carbide precipitation and sensitization, and silicon, which was probably added as a deoxidizer during processing, are indicated by minor peaks for S i  (~ 1.7 keV) and C (~ 0.3 keV) (Callister and Rethwisch  6 ). The spectrum matches the F e –C r -N i  system, indicating that the alloy is appropriate for uses that call for high corrosion resistance, especially in situations with a lot of chloride (Kutz  21 ). Impurities like Si and C highlight the need of precise compositional management since they affect weldability and the creation of defects like porosity or cracking during laser welding (Katayama  16 ).Given that C r  and N i  levels have a direct influence on temperature and phase transitions, which ensure the alloy's mechanical integrity, this elemental analysis offers crucial information for improving welding conditions (ASM International  4 ). These results demonstrate 304L stainless steel's great performance potential while emphasizing how crucial impurity control is to preserving its corrosion-resistant and structural qualities. It shows a more or less homogeneous shape made up of well-defined polygonal grains, typical of stainless steel 304 L. Additionally, it shows grain joints or delimitation lines that indicate complete recrystallization and good structural homogeneity. The presence of homogeneous chromium and nickel confirms the austenitic nature of the stainless 304L steel. EDS analyses were conducted to ensure the elements' chemical composition. S i  is sparse

Following mechanical U-bent deformation and immersion in a 20% HCI solution, the stainless steel 304L exhibits a microstructure that reveals typical corrosion phenomena under control. The electronic micrography at balance (MEB) (image 5) reveals a granular structure that is characteristic of austenitic steel, with areas where cracks and an accumulation of rugosity are visible. These cracks, which are primarily found along grain joints, indicate deterioration as a result of the combination of residual mechanical stresses caused by plastic deformation and the aggressive environment provided by solution acid (Luo et al.,  23 ). This phenomenon, often referred to as stress corrosion, frequently causes failure in stainless steel when they are exposed to environments that contain chloride ions (Fontana  12 ). Key chemical elements have an uneven distribution, according to chemical research using energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). Grain boundaries have a higher concentration of carbon (C-K) on elemental maps, suggesting the likely development of carbides (C r23 C 6 ).Sensitization causes these carbides, which lower the local chromium concentration (Cr-K) near grain borders, increasing their susceptibility to intergranular corrosion (Marcus  25 ). A relative reduction in the homogenous distribution of chromium confirms its localized disintegration. Furthermore, oxygen (O-K) mapping shows that extended exposure to hydrochloric acid results in the development of corrosion products, most likely metal oxides and chlorides (Scharfstein et al.,  31 ). Significant dissolving of iron (Fe-K) is also seen, frequently linked to the production of iron chlorides, which hasten the spread of cracks (Oldfield  29 ). However, nickel (Ni-K), which is essential for maintaining the austenitic phase, seems to be evenly distributed throughout the matrix, indicating that this phase is somewhat resistant to dissolution in an acidic media (Tuthill  36 ) (Fig.  5 ). Fig. 5 SEM image of 304L (scale bar: 10 um) with EDS maps (C, O, S i , C r , F e , N i ). Compared to Fig.  4 , F e /C r /N i  remain uniform with fewer O and C enrichments, indicating a cleaner/less oxidized surface

sections.heading: Tensile test
paragraphs: We wanted to examine how corrosion affected mechanical qualities, namely tensile strength, after researching stress corrosion of 304 l stainless steel. In order to do this, we submerged two tensile specimens in drinking water containing 20% of HCL for one and two months, respectively.

The resulting tensile curve in Fig.  6  illustrates how the mechanical characteristics of 304L stainless steel change in response to the conditions of being submerged in a corrosive environment. Three sets of curves are displayed. The red curve shows a specimen that was not immersed, the green curve shows a specimen that was submerged for a month, and the blue curve shows a specimen that was submerged for two months. Each curve provides a foundation for analyzing deterioration mechanisms by illuminating the steel's mechanical properties in terms of stress and elongation. The usual behavior of austenitic steels is depicted by the red curve, which depicts the specimen in its original, unimmersed form. Its low yield strength is one of its characteristics, after which there is a strain-hardening plateau where stress gradually rises as elongation increases. The greatest stress attained is around 500 MPa, and the total elongation exceeds 60%. These characteristics are a result of the nickel-stabilized austenitic phase's inherent strong mechanical strength and exceptional ductility (Luo et al.,  24 ). In the absence of chemical assault, the steel has great resistance to mechanical stress due to its homogenous microstructural structure and a protective passive layer that is rich in chromium (Fontana  12 ). The green curve indicates a significant decrease in maximal tensile strength and elongation at break following a month of submersion in water containing 20% HCL. Final elongation goes below 60%, and maximum stress marginally decreases. The emergence of localized corrosion processes including pitting and intergranular corrosion is responsible for these alterations (Marcus  25 ). Fig. 6 Engineering stress–strain curves for 304L: non-immersed (red) vs. 1-month (green) and 2-month (blue) immersion. Strength and ductility decrease with immersion time; the 2-month condition shows the largest loss

Local sensitization and a decrease in the steel's inherent passivity result from the selective dissolving of chromium at grain boundaries caused by corrosive assault in environments containing chloride ions (Scharfstein et al.,  31 ). Microstructural cohesiveness is weakened by these activities, increasing the matrix's vulnerability to mechanical breakdown under stress (Oldfield  29 ). The blue curve, representing the specimen after two months' immersion, shows more marked mechanical degradation. The maximum stress decreases further, reaching around 400 MPa, while the elongation at break falls significantly below 50%. These results reveal accelerated embrittlement due to cumulative corrosion phenomena. Prolonged exposure to chloride ions intensifies the dissolution processes of alloying elements, particularly chromium, and iron, favoring crack initiation and propagation (Tuthill  36 ). Chromium carbide precipitation causes grain boundaries to create crucial weak spots (C r23 C 6 ), depleting the surrounding chromium zones and reducing their resistance to intergranular corrosion (Uhlig  37 ). In addition, corrosion products that build up on the surface, such as metallic chlorides, aggravates the cracking mechanisms (Charles  8 ) (Fig.  7 ) (Table  2 ). The SEM pictures show how the microstructure of 304L stainless steel changed after being immersed in a corrosive solution containing 20% hydrochloric acid and then put through a tensile test. The three micrographs show, in order, (a) a specimen that was not submerged, (b) a specimen that was submerged for a month, and (c) a specimen that was submerged for two months. Significant variations in the fracture surfaces' morphology were found by the investigation, which demonstrated the combined impact of mechanical deformation and corrosion.1. The unsubmerged specimen's microstructure (Image a) displays a typical ductile fracture surface, which is characterized by morphology of uniformly distributed cavities (dimples). The dimpled fracture surface reflects microvoid coalescence and thus a predominantly ductile, overload type failure, which is consistent with the retained tensile ductility and inherent strength of 304L observed here (Callister and Rethwisch  6 ). This morphology contrasts with classic SCC signatures (intergranular facets, quasi cleavage, and dense secondary cracking) and indicates that, under the present conditions, SCC was not the dominant fracture mode. Nevertheless, the slight oxygen enrichment and inclusion associated features observed after two months, together with the measured loss in strength/elongation, are compatible with early stages of chloride assisted damage-namely pit initiation at M n S/inclusion sites and slip oxidation at active slip bands both of which are well recognized precursors to SCC in 304L under sustained tensile stress. In this alloy, SCC typically initiates via a pit to crack transition where local depassivation and acidification in the pit environment promote film rupture, anodic dissolution at the crack tip, and hydrogen uptake that lowers the barrier for localized plasticity. The absence of intergranular attack in our specimens further suggests no sensitization (chromium carbide precipitation) and aligns with a stabilized austenitic matrix, thereby explaining why the fracture remains largely ductile while still showing microstructural indicators that map onto established SCC initiation mechanisms for 304L in chloride media (Callister and Rethwisch  6 ; Marcus  25 ). A fracture surface with multiple characteristics may be seen in image b. Areas of fracture start and indications of intergranular deterioration coexist with the dimples, which are still discernible. The presence of an embedded foreign particle in the fracture zone, most likely a corrosion product, suggests that the corrosive solution has attacked locally. This shape is typical of pitting corrosion and stress corrosion cracking (SCC), which are frequently seen in situations with a lot of chloride ions (Marcus  25 ). By decreasing grain cohesiveness and serving as stress concentrators, corrosion products such metal chlorides encourage local embrittlement (ASTM  5 ). The metal matrix becomes mechanically weaker and more prone to deformation when grain boundaries rupture too soon (Oldfield  29 ).Advanced deterioration can be seen in image c. The morphology of the fracture surface is characterized by increased roughness and extensive intergranular fissures. There are now obvious indications of intergranular corrosion in place of the dimples that are typical of ductile fractures. Additionally, visible is a corrosion product particle, indicating that the chemicals generated play a crucial role in accelerating deterioration (Fontana  12 ).This morphology shows that a sustained chemical treatment has caused a fracture to change from ductile to brittle. Sensitization causes chromium carbides (C r23  Cg) to precipitate at grain boundaries, depleting the chromium in these regions, decreasing corrosion resistance, and hastening cracking (Uhlig  37 ). The alloying elements' selective dissolution is prolonged under service conditions in an acidic environment, which makes the material more brittle (Tuthill  36 ).

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: In conclusion, Utilizing U-bent 304L austenitic stainless steel immersed in a 20% HCl solution for one and two months yields significant new knowledge on the mechanisms of stress corrosion cracking (SCC) in hostile chloride environments. The initial U-bend deformation, applied to simulate tensile stress, created localized microstructural alterations, evident through surface irregularities, microcracks, and deformation bands, which served as potential SCC initiation sites. After one month of immersion, the microstructure exhibited noticeable signs of localized corrosion, such as pitting and grain boundary attack, indicating an early breakdown of the passive film. This early-stage degradation aligns with findings in the literature, where chloride ions are known to penetrate weakened areas and initiate localized attacks through the dissolution of the passive.

The development of SCC became more noticeable once the immersion was prolonged to two months, as evidenced by wider and deeper holes and obvious deposits that were signs of corrosion products. Long-term exposure to chlorinated environments has been linked to chromium depletion at grain boundaries, which increases intergranular corrosion and encourages the spread of cracks in areas where stress is concentrated. This advanced degree of degradation is consistent with these findings.

The findings support previous studies that demonstrate how mechanical stress and a high chloride environment significantly reduce 304L stainless steel's resistance to corrosion, particularly in deformed regions.

These results provide credence to a preventative toolset for 304L in chloride service from an industrial perspective: specify low-C "L" grades and solution-annealed conditions, prevent sensitization, and reduce residual tensile stress by using compressive-stress treatments (such as micro/laser shot-peening) on cold-worked zones and welds, large bend radii, and stress-relief when practical; regulate the environment by preventing chloride deposition and wet-dry cycles, avoiding the 50–150 °C range that is favorable for CI–SCC in the presence of moisture, controlling RH/condensation, and removing stagnant traps and crevices; improve the barrier by thorough post-weld cleaning, passivation, and fine surface polishing or electro polishing, Choose up-alloying (such as 316L, 904L, or duplex grades) for better localized corrosion resistance when risk is still high. Lastly, use condition-based monitoring (replica inspections, pit/crack density metrics linked to acceptance limits, AE or EC NDT on critical components, and periodic SEM/replica inspections) with documented replacement/maintenance intervals triggered by quantified loss in ductility or growth in damage indicators.

This work underscores the vulnerability of 304L stainless steel to SCC in high-chloride environments, especially under mechanical deformation, and highlights the need for additional research into protective strategies, such as alloying or surface treatments, to enhance its resistance in such conditions. A basis for understanding the behavior of SCC in austenitic stainless steels is provided by the degradation mechanisms that have been identified, such as intergranular attack and passive layer disruption. This supports the ongoing creation of materials that are resistant to corrosion and may be used in difficult situations.
